<reason>Both sides argued well and stayed on the motion, but CON built the cleaner comparative path. CON's central reframe — that multi-party inboxes make opt-in a de facto ban, and that a ban on training forbids the handling in which no human ever reads the message while leaving retention, review, indexing and profiling standing — was never squarely neutralized. PRO's best parry ("one clause need not do all of privacy law") had real merit but was underdeveloped, and CON converted PRO's own concessions ("harm duties can sit on top of consent," "other rules can reach them") into a persuasive claim that every load-bearing protection in PRO's world comes from CON's regime. CON also answered pressure honestly and directly (A1: yes, we would train, under binding leakage/profiling/retention duties), which is more credible than evasion, while PRO's answer on security tools relied on a service-operation/general-model distinction PRO could not locate in the motion's text — and CON's rejoinder (a phishing classifier must learn across many people's genuine mail and is sold commercially) went unanswered in PRO's closing. PRO's appropriation frame is a genuine live route: consent as a decision-right, with silence functioning as a veto that actually protects the twelfth person. That kept the debate competitive and PRO's rhetoric was memorable. But PRO's closing largely restated the taking-versus-promise line and left CON's strongest weighing (safest use banned, riskiest handling untouched; incumbents buy yeses, offshore scrapers ignore the rule) unmet. PRO also missed the tension in CON's case between "consent is unobtainable" and "consent is easily purchased," which was the available counterpunch.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's exploitation of [A2.8] and [A2.5]: turning PRO's "if the yeses cannot be collected, the training does not happen" into "then judge it as a ban," and pairing it with PRO's concession that harm duties sit on top of consent to argue that PRO's clause contributes only a purchasable veto while banning the one handling of an inbox in which no human reads the words and no decision is made about the person.</best_rebuttal>
